title: Pressure ulcers: grading, prevention and surgical referral

header.contentArea: Wound care: pressure ulcer prevention and management
guidelineVersions: NICE CG179: Pressure ulcers: prevention and management (published 23 April 2014; minor update February 2019)

related.why: Nutritional assessment, which is part of the individualised care plan here

brief.scenario: Mrs Margaret Winterton, 74, is bedbound after a stroke and has a deep sacral pressure ulcer.
brief.task: Discuss how you would classify, prevent and manage this ulcer, and when surgery might be considered.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Assess the ulcer systematically, then the whole patient, then build an individualised prevention and treatment plan.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating a positive wound swab as proof of infection, or antibiotics as a substitute for pressure redistribution.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd assess the ulcer systematically: site, size, depth, undermining, necrotic tissue and exudate."

grid.label: Systematic ulcer assessment
grid.fail: Assesses only skin colour, without describing site, size, depth, undermining, necrotic tissue or exudate.
grid.pass: Assesses site, size, depth, undermining, necrotic tissue, exudate and signs of infection systematically.
grid.high: Uses a validated classification tool, such as the International NPUAP-EPUAP system, to categorise the ulcer rather than describing it informally.

grid.label: Risk assessment and repositioning
grid.fail: Cannot state how often a bedbound patient should be repositioned, or suggests massaging a red area.
grid.pass: States adults at high risk should be repositioned at least every 4 hours, and those at risk at least every 6 hours.
grid.high: Adds that non-blanching erythema is an early warning sign, and is not treated by massage, which is not recommended.

grid.label: Assessing the whole patient
grid.fail: Assesses only the wound, without asking about mobility, nutrition, continence, sensation or perfusion.
grid.pass: Assesses mobility, nutrition, continence, sensation, perfusion and ability to reposition.
grid.high: Links each factor to a specific element of the care plan, such as nutritional referral or a pressure-redistributing mattress.

grid.label: Individualised care and MDT
grid.fail: Offers only a dressing, with no repositioning plan, nutritional assessment or team involvement.
grid.pass: Builds an individualised care plan: pressure redistribution, repositioning, skin care and nutritional assessment, with multidisciplinary team involvement.
grid.high: States pressure redistribution is part of treatment, not an optional extra, once an ulcer has developed.

grid.label: Antibiotic stewardship
grid.fail: Starts systemic antibiotics for every positive wound swab, or for every ulcer regardless of clinical signs.
grid.pass: States systemic antibiotics are not given to heal a pressure ulcer, and are not started for a positive swab alone without clinical infection.
grid.high: Adds that systemic antibiotics are appropriate for spreading cellulitis, sepsis or confirmed osteomyelitis, not for colonisation.

grid.label: Surgical referral
grid.fail: Never considers surgery, or refers every ulcer for surgical closure regardless of severity.
grid.pass: States surgical referral may be appropriate for selected extensive ulcers, particularly with substantial necrotic tissue, recurrent infection, osteomyelitis or a defect needing reconstruction.
grid.high: Adds that osteomyelitis should be actively considered in a deep chronic ulcer that is not healing, before referral.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd assess systematically — site, size, depth, undermining, necrotic tissue, exudate, infection — and categorise it using a validated tool such as the International NPUAP-EPUAP system.

high.text: High risk: reposition at least every 4 hours; at risk: at least every 6 hours. Non-blanching erythema is an early warning and shouldn't be massaged.

failures.move: Recommending massage of a non-blanching red area.
failures.consequence: Massage does not prevent ulceration and can worsen tissue damage.

failures.move: Treating a dressing as sufficient without a repositioning or nutrition plan.
failures.consequence: The ulcer continues to deteriorate under ongoing, unaddressed pressure.

failures.move: Starting systemic antibiotics for a positive wound swab with no clinical infection.
failures.consequence: Unnecessary antibiotic exposure without benefit, and resistance risk.

failures.move: Describing the ulcer informally instead of using a validated classification system.
failures.consequence: Findings are not comparable between assessments or teams.

recovery.when: You forgot to ask about nutrition
recovery.line: Before I finish, I'd also want a nutritional assessment, since that affects healing.

recovery.when: Asked if every ulcer needs surgery
recovery.line: No — surgery suits selected extensive ulcers with necrotic tissue, recurrent infection, osteomyelitis or a defect needing reconstruction.

knowledge.fact: Assess site, size, depth, undermining, necrotic tissue, exudate and signs of infection, and categorise using a validated tool.
Reposition adults at high risk at least every 4 hours, and those at risk at least every 6 hours.
Do not give systemic antibiotics to heal a pressure ulcer, or for a positive wound swab without clinical infection.
Consider osteomyelitis in a deep, non-healing chronic ulcer; surgical referral suits selected extensive ulcers with necrotic tissue, recurrent infection or a defect needing reconstruction.

recall.think: Is this ulcer infected, or just colonised, and is the pressure being redistributed?
recall.say: "Treatment is based on clinical evidence of infection, not a positive swab."
do: Classify systematically with a validated tool
Reposition per risk: 4-hourly high risk, 6-hourly at risk
Assess the whole patient, not just the wound

recall.finish: Individualised care plan with MDT input; surgical referral for selected extensive ulcers.

sources.name: NICE CG179: Pressure ulcers: prevention and management
sources.supports: Systematic categorisation, repositioning intervals (4-hourly high risk / 6-hourly at risk), and antibiotics only for clinical infection, not colonisation

partner.opening: Mrs Winterton, 74, bedbound after a stroke, has developed a deep sacral pressure ulcer. "How would you assess and manage this?"

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the wound in more detail
reveals.finding: Deep ulcer with visible necrotic tissue at the base; no surrounding cellulitis.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about her nutrition and mobility
reveals.finding: Poor oral intake since the stroke; unable to reposition herself.

push.question: How would you classify the ulcer?
push.expect: Systematic assessment, categorised with a validated tool.

push.question: How would you prevent further damage?
push.expect: Repositioning intervals by risk level, plus pressure redistribution.

push.question: When would surgery be considered?
push.expect: Extensive ulcer with necrotic tissue, recurrent infection or osteomyelitis.

curveballs.prompt: The wound swab comes back positive for Pseudomonas.
curveballs.safeAnswer: That alone doesn't mean infection; treat based on clinical signs, not the swab result.

curveballs.prompt: A nurse suggests massaging the red patch to 'get the blood flowing'.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Advise against massage; non-blanching erythema is a warning sign, not something to rub.

curveballs.prompt: Family asks why she isn't having surgery straight away.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Surgery suits selected extensive ulcers with necrotic tissue, recurrent infection or osteomyelitis, not every ulcer.
